    Reference Validation Pipeline and Scoring

    reference-validation-pipeline.Rmd

    Introduction

    This page presents the validation of bibliographic references: comparing extracted references (by GROBID or by APA 7 regular expressions) with online metadata databases (OpenAlex and doi.org), and measuring how well they match.

    It follows the logical order of a complete workflow:

    1. Prepare the references in a format compatible with validation (preliminary step, briefly recalled);
    2. Validate with validate_references() and interpret its output;
    3. Understand how the scores are computed (title, authors, year, global score) and their known limitations;
    4. Tune the validation parameters with oa_matching_info() and checkrefr_set_defaults();
    5. Examine the author score in detail with compute_author_score() and sim_author_pair();
    6. Deduplicate the result with deduplicate_references().

    Caution. As noted on the Get started page, the current version of the package is experimental and the score computation method is under revision. Scores and statuses are decision aids, not a verdict: manual verification remains necessary for ambiguous cases. Known limitations are detailed in the section “Known limitations of the current formula” below.

    Preliminary step: preparing the references

    validate_references() expects a table of references in a specific format. Two routes can produce it. Their operation is presented on other pages; they are recalled here to provide a complete pipeline.

    Source of references Function(s) Result
    PDF or text files processed by GROBID grobid_process_file() or grobid_process_files() Directly compatible table
    References in APA 7 format (plain text) parse_apa_text(..., as_ref_df = TRUE) (equivalent to parse_apa_text() followed by format_apa_for_validation()) Compatible table

    GROBID route 

    ref_path <- system.file("extdata", "ref_test.txt", package = "CheckrefR")

res <- grobid_process_file(
  file = ref_path,
  mode = "remote",
  model_type = "crf"
)

refs <- res$references

    APA 7 route 

    refs <- parse_apa_text(ref_path, as_ref_df = TRUE)

    Expected format

    In both cases, the refs table contains (at minimum) the following columns:

    Column Content
    raw_reference Raw text of the reference
    source_file Name of the original file
    ref_n Number of the reference within that file
    title Extracted title
    authors Authors as text
    authors_list Authors as a structured list (first name, last name)
    doi Extracted DOI, if any
    year Year of publication

    One row = one reference. The source_file + ref_n pair uniquely identifies each reference. This key is what later allows results to be grouped and deduplicated (see the last section).

    Validating references: validate_references()

    General principle

    For each reference, the function queries OpenAlex (a large open database of scientific publications) and, if needed, doi.org (the service that resolves DOIs), then compares the metadata found with those of the original reference.

    The logic unfolds in two stages:

    1. DOI validation (if the reference has one). Syntactically valid DOIs are first looked up in OpenAlex, in batches. Those not found there are then queried individually on doi.org.
    2. Title validation. The title is searched in OpenAlex, either in addition to the DOI (if it was not sufficient) or in its place (if there is none).

    Each candidate found receives matching scores (title, authors, year, global) and a status summarizing the result.

    validated <- validate_references(refs)
    Argument Role Default value
    refs Table of references in the format described above (required)
    verbose Displays progress and a final summary TRUE
    max_candidates Maximum number of candidates kept per reference 3 (setting oa_max_candidates) 
    
checkrefr_set_defaults(oa_api_key = keyring::key_get("openalex"))
#> ✔ Variable(s) updated: "oa_api_key"

cache_file <- "validated_refs.rds"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  validated <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  ref_path <- system.file("extdata", "ref_test.txt", package = "CheckrefR")
  refs <- parse_apa_text(ref_path, as_ref_df = TRUE)
  validated <- validate_references(refs)
  saveRDS(validated, cache_file)
}

    Network and duration. Validation requires an Internet connection and can take time depending on the number of references. Requests are sent in batches with a short pause between each, and temporary errors are automatically retried.

    OpenAlex API key and email address

    validate_references() queries the OpenAlex API. For regular use, it is strongly recommended to provide two pieces of information, once per session, with checkrefr_set_defaults():

    checkrefr_set_defaults(
  oa_api_key = "YOUR_OPENALEX_KEY",
  doi_email  = "firstname.lastname@example.org"
)
    Parameter Role
    oa_api_key Personal OpenAlex API key, sent with each request
    doi_email Your email address, sent to OpenAlex (mailto parameter) and to the other services queried (doi.org) in the request identification

    Obtaining an OpenAlex API key.

    1. Create a (free) account on openalex.org.
    2. Log in, then open the Settings page of your account to generate your API key.
    3. Copy the key and pass it to the package with checkrefr_set_defaults(oa_api_key = "...").

    Usage limits. The OpenAlex API applies rate limits (number of requests per second and per day) and, depending on its current policy, may require users to identify themselves for regular use. These rules change and are not managed by CheckrefR: consult the official OpenAlex rate limits page for current values.

    Without a key. Validation works, but you share the anonymous quota, which is more restricted. If it is exceeded, the server responds “429 Too Many Requests”: the package then automatically retries the request (up to 5 attempts, with increasing wait times). If the failure persists, the references concerned are treated as not found, which can skew results on large volumes.

    With a key. You benefit from the limits associated with your account, which is preferable for validating long lists of references.

    Tips for large volumes. Validate in batches of references rather than all at once, keep intermediate results with saveRDS(), and watch the messages displayed during processing: a message reporting a batch that failed after several attempts means the DOIs concerned will be considered not found.

    To check the active configuration, use oa_matching_info(): the key appears under the heading “API key (oa_api_key)”, or “(not set)” if it is not defined.

    Reading the result

    The result contains one row per retained candidate, so a reference may appear on several rows (up to max_candidates).

    The output of validate_references() contains the following columns, in this order:

    Column Content
    source_file Name of the reference’s original file
    ref_n Number of the reference within that file
    input_title Title extracted from your reference
    input_doi DOI extracted from your reference
    input_year Year extracted from your reference
    input_authors Authors extracted from your reference
    oa_id OpenAlex identifier of the candidate found
    oa_title Title of the candidate
    oa_doi DOI of the candidate
    oa_year Year of the candidate
    oa_authors Authors of the candidate
    score_title Title similarity (0 to 1)
    score_authors Author list similarity (0 to 1)
    score_year Year match (0, 0.5 or 1)
    score_global Weighted global score (0 to 1)
    n_candidates Number of candidates retained for this reference
    match_status Match status (see table below)
    raw_reference Raw text of the original reference

    Columns prefixed with input_ describe your reference, while those prefixed with oa_ describe the candidate found (OpenAlex or doi.org). When no candidate is found (no_match), the oa_* columns and the scores are empty.

    validated |>
  select(ref_n, input_title, oa_title, score_title, score_authors,
         score_year, score_global, match_status) |>
  head(8) |>
  kable_site(
    caption = "Preview of the validation result",
    digits = 2
  )

    Match statuses (match_status)

    Status Meaning
    confirmed_with_doi The DOI leads to a work with the same year and a very close title (similarity of at least oa_doi_threshold, 0.90 by default). Strong match.
    partial_with_doi The DOI exists and leads to a work that is broadly compatible (global score of at least oa_min_threshold), but the year or title is not enough to confirm. To be checked.
    doi_mismatch The DOI exists, but the work found does not sufficiently match the reference (global score below oa_min_threshold). Suggests a DOI associated with another publication.
    doi_does_not_exist doi.org indicates that this DOI does not exist.
    title_search Candidate found by title search in OpenAlex (reference without a DOI, or inconclusive DOI).
    no_match No sufficiently close candidate was found. The oa_* columns and the scores are empty.

    Generative AI error scenarios. These statuses make it possible to detect the cases described in Get started:

    • real reference, wrong DOI: doi_mismatch or doi_does_not_exist, often accompanied by a title_search candidate with a good score;
    • real DOI, wrong reference: doi_mismatch (the DOI points to a different article);
    • entirely fabricated reference: no_match;
    • partially accurate reference: partial_with_doi, or a title_search status with an intermediate global score.

  count(match_status, name = "n_rows") |>
  arrange(desc(n_rows)) |>

    Putting it in perspective: a test reference set with known ground truth

    The example file ref_test.txt was built to illustrate the different scenarios that validation must distinguish. It contains 14 references whose true status is known in advance, which makes it possible to compare what the package returns with what is expected.

    The references fall into four categories:

    Category Description References
    1. Correct Real reference, accurate metadata (article, conference paper, preprint, book, chapter) 1 to 5
    2. Misattributed DOI The DOI exists and works, but points to a different article than the one cited (both publications are real) 6 and 7
    3. Fabricated DOI The DOI does not exist, but the rest of the reference is accurate 8 and 9
    4. Nonexistent Entirely false reference: level 1 (gross inconsistencies) or level 2 (plausible, close to a real reference) 10 to 14
    Click to display the detailed list of the 14 references used for the test

    This list presents the exact text of each reference in the ref_test.txt file, grouped by category, with details on the nature of the error introduced.

    Category 1: references correct in every respect

    1. Research article

    Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The “what” and “why” of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior. Psychological Inquiry, 11(4), 227–268. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15327965PLI1104_01

    2. Conference paper

    Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space. In Y. Bengio & Y. LeCun (Eds.), Proceedings of the 1st International Conference on Learning Representations (pp. 1–12). ICLR.

    3. Preprint

    Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention is all you need. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762

    The DOI is real and functional, but it points to a different article than the one cited. Both publications actually exist.

    Examples of each category

    Category 1: correct. Deci & Ryan (2000), “The ‘what’ and ‘why’ of goal pursuits…”, with its exact DOI. We expect a confirmed_with_doi status and scores close to 1. References without a DOI (conference paper, book, chapter) go through title search: we expect title_search, with a score that varies depending on how well OpenAlex covers these document types.

    Category 2: misattributed DOI. Bandura (1977), “Self-efficacy…”, associated with the DOI 10.1037/0003-066X.55.1.5, which actually corresponds to Seligman & Csikszentmihalyi (2000). Both publications exist, but do not belong together. We expect doi_mismatch, possibly accompanied by a title_search candidate corresponding to the true reference.

    Category 3: fabricated DOI. Rogers (1957), “The necessary and sufficient conditions…”, with a nonexistent DOI (10.1037/h9999999): the rest of the reference is accurate. We expect doi_does_not_exist or doi_not_found, then a good candidate found by title.

    Category 4, level 1: obviously false. Dupont & Tremblay (2019), “L’influence quantique de la pensée positive…”. We expect no_match.

    Category 4, level 2: false but plausible. Kahneman & Tversky (1984), “Thinking, slow and fast”, very close to Kahneman’s real reference (2011). This is the trickiest case: a title close to a real work can produce an intermediate score and a misleading title_search candidate.

    How to read this comparison

    Compare, row by row, the expected category with the status obtained:

    • references in category 1 should have high scores and a matching status (confirmed_with_doi or title_search);
    • those in categories 2 and 3 should show a DOI-related status (doi_mismatch, doi_does_not_exist, doi_not_found);
    • those in category 4 should be no_match, or else obtain markedly lower scores than the correct references.

    What this test shows, and what it does not. It illustrates the package’s behavior on only 14 cases, chosen for their pedagogical value: it is neither a statistical evaluation of the method nor a measure of its reliability. Level 2 cases (false references close to real ones) and references without a DOI (books, chapters, conference papers) are the most sensitive: an intermediate score does not allow a conclusion, and manual verification remains necessary.

    Score computation

    Overview

    Each candidate receives three partial scores, all between 0 (no resemblance) and 1 (identical), then a global score that combines them.

    ⚠️ Experimental version. The formula presented here is the one currently implemented. It is under revision and has limitations (see below). Stay vigilant when interpreting it. More formal tests are planned.

    Title score

    The two titles (that of your reference and that of the candidate) are first normalized: conversion to lowercase, removal of accents, replacement of any character other than an unaccented letter, a digit or a space with a space, and collapsing of multiple spaces.

    The score is then a string similarity based on the Damerau-Levenshtein distance:

    Stitle=1−dDL(t1,t2)max⁡(|t1|,|t2|) S_{\text{title}} = 1 - \frac{d_{DL}(t_1,\, t_2)}{\max(|t_1|,\, |t_2|)}

    In plain terms: dDLd_{DL} counts the minimum number of edits (inserting, deleting or replacing a character, or swapping two adjacent characters) needed to transform one title into the other. This number is divided by the length of the longer title, then subtracted from 1. Two identical titles score 1; the more they differ, the closer the score gets to 0. If one of the titles is missing, the score is 0.

    Year score

    Syear={1if |a1−a2|=00.5if |a1−a2|=10otherwise (or if a year is missing) S_{\text{year}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |a_1 - a_2| = 0 \\ 0.5 & \text{if } |a_1 - a_2| = 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise (or if a year is missing)} \end{cases}

    In plain terms: identical year, 1; one year apart, 0.5 (tolerance for publications whose online and print volume dates differ); beyond that, 0.

    Author score

    The author score is computed by comparing authors pairwise, then taking the average of these comparisons:

    Sauthors=1n∑i=1ns(ai,bi) S_{\text{authors}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} s(a_i,\, b_i)

    In plain terms: we take the nn author pairs compared (the ii-th author of your reference with the ii-th author of the candidate), compute a similarity score ss for each pair, then average them. The detail of the computation for one pair is given below (sim_author_pair()). Additional rules (lists of different lengths, truncated lists) are described in the section dedicated to compute_author_score().

    Global score

    Sglobal=wt⋅Stitle+wa⋅Sauthors+wy⋅Syear S_{\text{global}} = w_t \cdot S_{\text{title}} + w_a \cdot S_{\text{authors}} + w_y \cdot S_{\text{year}}

    with default values wt=0.60w_t = 0.60, wa=0.30w_a = 0.30 and wy=0.10w_y = 0.10.

    In plain terms: the global score is a weighted average. The title counts for 60%, the authors for 30% and the year for 10%. If the three weights do not sum exactly to 1, they are automatically rescaled to sum to 1 before the computation.

    # Illustration with the default weights
s_title <- 0.95; s_authors <- 0.80; s_year <- 1

0.60 * s_title + 0.30 * s_authors + 0.10 * s_year
#> [1] 0.91

    How candidates are retained

    1. Candidates whose global score is below oa_min_threshold (0.60 by default) are discarded (except for candidates coming from a DOI, whose status is then determined as described above);
    2. the remaining candidates are sorted from best to worst;
    3. the best one is always kept;
    4. the following ones are kept only if they reach oa_probable_threshold (0.85 by default);
    5. the total is capped at max_candidates.

    Known limitations of the current formula

    ⚠️ Author score: points of caution.

    1. One score per author, then an average. The author score is not computed on the list as a whole: it is the average of the scores of each author taken individually. A false positive on a single author therefore does not carry the same weight depending on the size of the list: it weighs heavily in a two-author reference, and very little in a twenty-author reference. The impact of the bias described below therefore varies with the number of authors.

    2. Lax bias: a single shared word is enough. An author receives a score of at least 0.8 out of 1 as soon as at least one element of their name (one “word” of the family name, generally) is identical in both sources. Two genuinely different compound names can thus be considered matching on the basis of just one part of the surname. The risk is particularly marked for names with a particle (van, de, der, von…) or with several elements: a common particle, or a single shared element, can be enough to produce a match.

    3. Strict bias: accents and special characters. Conversely, the comparison is made word by word and requires an exact match of characters. The slightest difference between two words (an accent present in one source and absent in the other, for example) causes those words to be considered different. Yet the diacritics of an author’s name often vary between sources: a genuine match may then go unrecognized.

    Practical consequence. A high author score does not prove that the author lists match, and a low score may simply reflect variations in how names are spelled. For high-stakes references, look at the input_authors and oa_authors columns side by side.

    Tuning the validation

    Viewing the settings: oa_matching_info()

    This function displays the parameters currently used for validation and returns them (invisibly) as a list.

    info <- oa_matching_info()

    The returned list contains five groups of parameters:

    Element Content
    thresholds Decision thresholds
    weights Global score weights
    query_controls Number of candidates and OpenAlex API key
    author_window Window-based comparison settings and large-list settings
    truncation Coverage and penalty settings for truncated lists

    Changing the settings: checkrefr_set_defaults()

    Settings are changed with checkrefr_set_defaults(), for the current session (see the GROBID Server Setup and Administration page for the general principle and for resetting).

    checkrefr_set_defaults(
  oa_min_threshold = 0.55,
  oa_w_title       = 0.70,
  oa_w_authors     = 0.20,
  oa_w_year        = 0.10
)

    Thresholds

    Parameter Role Default
    oa_min_threshold Minimum global score required to retain a candidate. Also used to distinguish partial_with_doi from doi_mismatch. 0.60
    oa_probable_threshold Global score required to keep additional candidates beyond the best one. 0.85
    oa_doi_threshold Title similarity threshold required (with an identical year) to confirm a DOI match (confirmed_with_doi). 0.90

    Weights

    Parameter Role Default
    oa_w_title Weight of the title in the global score 0.60
    oa_w_authors Weight of the authors 0.30
    oa_w_year Weight of the year 0.10

    Queries

    Parameter Role Default
    oa_max_candidates Maximum number of candidates retained per reference 3
    oa_api_key OpenAlex API key (optional) not set
    doi_email Email address sent to the services queried (good practice for “polite” access) not set
    doi_max_retries Maximum number of attempts for doi.org in case of a network or server error 3
    doi_retry_backoff Initial delay between two attempts (seconds), doubled with each new attempt 1

    Author list comparison

    Parameter Role Default
    oa_large_author_threshold OpenAlex list size from which a comparison with a very short list (2 authors or fewer) is considered indeterminate (score of 0) 10
    oa_sym_max_diff_abs Maximum absolute length difference between two lists for them to be considered of comparable length 2
    oa_sym_max_diff_prop Maximum relative length difference for them to be considered of comparable length 0.10
    oa_min_coverage_ratio Minimum share of the longer list covered by the shorter one for a penalty to be applied 0.65
    oa_author_lambda Intensity of the penalty applied to lists of different lengths 0.4
    oa_use_window Enables window-based comparison (instead of a strictly position-by-position comparison) FALSE
    oa_window_size Half-width of the window (number of positions before and after) 2

    Weights. The three weights are automatically rescaled to sum to 1 if they do not already. The default values should be considered provisional: the scoring method is under revision.

    The author score in detail

    Comparing two lists: compute_author_score()

    compute_author_score() computes the author score for two lists of names. It is used automatically by validate_references(), but can be called on its own to test a case.

    Argument Role
    ng List (vector) of the authors of your reference
    no List (vector) of the authors of the candidate (OpenAlex or doi.org)
    truncation_detected Indicates that your reference’s list is probably truncated (e.g. “et al.”)
    Other arguments Same settings as in checkrefr_set_defaults() (see previous table) 
    ng <- c("Smith, J.", "Doe, A.", "Martin, P.")
no <- c("John Smith", "Alice Doe", "Pierre Martin")

compute_author_score(ng, no)
#> [1] 1

    Rules depending on list size

    • Lists of comparable length (difference of at most oa_sym_max_diff_abs authors, or relative difference of at most oa_sym_max_diff_prop): authors are compared position by position, and the average is taken.
    • Lists of different lengths: the comparison covers the number of authors in the shorter list (position by position, or by window if oa_use_window = TRUE). If the shorter list covers at least oa_min_coverage_ratio of the longer one, the score is reduced by a penalty proportional to the lack of coverage, modulated by oa_author_lambda.
    • Truncated list (truncation_detected = TRUE, for example a reference that ends with “et al.”): when your list is the shorter one, no penalty is applied.
    • Indeterminate case: if your list has 2 authors or fewer against a list of oa_large_author_threshold authors or more, the score is set to 0 (comparison deemed uninformative).
    ng_short <- c("Smith, J.", "Doe, A.")
no_long  <- c("John Smith", "Alice Doe", "Pierre Martin", "Marie Curie")

# No truncation indicated: penalty applied
compute_author_score(ng_short, no_long)
#> [1] 1

# List known to be truncated ("et al."): no penalty
compute_author_score(ng_short, no_long, truncation_detected = TRUE)
#> [1] 1

    Comparing two authors: sim_author_pair()

    sim_author_pair() compares two author names and returns a score between 0 and 1.

    sim_author_pair("Smith, J.", "John Smith")
#> [1] 1
sim_author_pair("Smith, J.", "Smith, A.")
#> [1] 0.8
sim_author_pair("Smith, J.", "Doe, A.")
#> [1] 0

    Comparison steps

    1. Each name is normalized: lowercase, removal of commas and semicolons, hyphens treated as separators, splitting into words, and distinction between full words (surname, first name) and initials.
    2. The full words of the two names are compared: we look for those that are identical.
    3. The score follows from the result:

    s(a,b)={0if no full word is shared0.8+0.2×Jotherwise s(a, b) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if no full word is shared} \\ 0.8 + 0.2 \times J & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

    In plain terms: with no shared full word, the two names do not match (0). As soon as a single full word is shared, the score starts at 0.8. The remaining 0.2 depends on how close the remaining initials are (JJ is the Jaccard index: the share of common initials among all the initials of both names, from 0 to 1). Thus, an identical surname and initial give 1; the same family name with different initials gives 0.8.

    Link with the limitations. It is this “0.8 as soon as one full word is shared” rule that explains the lax bias described above. The exact word-by-word comparison (without accent harmonization) explains the strict bias.

    same_position = FALSE mode. Used for window-based comparison, it replaces the previous rule with an F1-type score: we count the share of words (full words and initials) in common relative to each of the two names, then combine the two proportions into a harmonic mean. The result remains between 0 and 1.

    Deduplicating the results: deduplicate_references()

    Since validate_references() can return several candidates per reference, deduplicate_references() keeps only the best candidate for each reference, that is, the one with the highest score_global.

    best <- deduplicate_references(validated, verbose = TRUE)
#> 
#> ── Summary by status
#> confirmed_with_doi: 2
#> doi_does_not_exist: 3
#> no_match: 1
#> title_search: 8
    Argument Role Default
    data Output of validate_references() (columns source_file, ref_n and score_global required) (required)
    verbose Displays a summary of the deduplication TRUE

    How it works

    • rows are grouped by reference (source_file + ref_n pair);
    • within each group, the row with the highest global score is kept; a missing score is treated as the lowest;
    • in case of a tie, the first row encountered is retained;
    • columns remain unchanged and the original row order is preserved.
    data.frame(
  Table = c("Before deduplication", "After deduplication"),
  Rows = c(nrow(validated), nrow(best)),
  `Distinct references` = c(
    n_distinct(validated $ source_file, validated $ ref_n),
    n_distinct(best $ source_file, best $ ref_n)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  kable_site(caption = "Effect of deduplicate_references()")
    Effect of deduplicate_references()
    Table Rows Distinct references
    Before deduplication 30 14
    After deduplication 14 14 
    best |>
  select(ref_n, input_title, oa_title, score_global, match_status) |>
  head(8) |>
  kable_site(
    caption = "Best candidate per reference",
    digits = 2
  )
    Best candidate per reference
    ref_n input_title oa_title score_global match_status
    1 The “what” and “why” of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior The “What” and “Why” of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior 0.97 confirmed_with_doi
    2 Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space 0.99 title_search
    3 Attention is all you need Attention Is All You Need 0.99 confirmed_with_doi
    4 Thinking, fast and slow Thinking, Fast and Slow 0.97 title_search
    5 The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation. 0.97 title_search
    6 Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change. 1.00 title_search
    7 Development and validation of brief measures of positive and negative affect: The PANAS scales Development and validation of brief measures of positive and negative affect: The PANAS scales. 0.99 title_search
    8 The necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic personality change The necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic personality change. 0.97 title_search

    Good to know. Deduplication chooses the candidate with the highest global score, which inherits the score limitations described above. A higher score is not a guarantee of a match: examine the match_status and compare the input and output metadata, especially for intermediate scores.

    Quickly checking whether DOIs exist

    validate_references() compares a reference with full metadata. Sometimes a simpler question is enough: does this DOI actually exist? That is the role of check_doi_exists(), a quick, standalone check, useful for instance to immediately spot fabricated DOIs (category 3 of the test set).

    What is the difference with validate_references()? check_doi_exists() answers only “yes”, “no” or “undetermined” to the question of whether a DOI exists. It compares neither the title, nor the authors, nor the year: a DOI that exists but is assigned to the wrong reference (category 2) will therefore be declared “existing”. To detect this case, you must use validate_references(). Moreover, the function is not called internally by validate_references(), which uses its own querying path (OpenAlex, then doi.org).

    Usage 

    check_doi_exists("10.1126/science.169.3946.635")

    The function accepts a DOI in several forms, which it normalizes automatically (spaces removed, lowercase, prefixes stripped):

    check_doi_exists("10.1126/science.169.3946.635")
check_doi_exists("https://doi.org/10.1126/science.169.3946.635")
check_doi_exists("doi:10.1126/science.169.3946.635")

    It is vectorized: it accepts a vector of DOIs and returns a vector of the same length, in the same order.

    dois <- c(
  "10.1126/science.169.3946.635",    # real DOI
  "10.9999/this-doi-does-not-exist", # valid syntax, nonexistent DOI
  "not_a_doi_at_all",                # string that is not a DOI
  NA                                 # missing value
)

check_doi_exists(dois)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE    NA    NA

    With named = TRUE, the elements of the result carry the normalized DOI as a name, which makes reading easier:

    check_doi_exists(dois, named = TRUE)

    Interpreting the result

    Value Meaning
    TRUE The DOI exists and resolves correctly
    FALSE The DOI is syntactically valid, but it does not exist, or the request failed (network unavailable, timeout)
    NA The element is missing or does not have the form of a DOI: no request is sent

    Beware of the FALSE value. It covers two situations: a genuinely nonexistent DOI, and a technical failure of the request (for example a dropped connection). Before concluding that a DOI is false, make sure your connection is working, for example by first testing a known DOI such as 10.1126/science.169.3946.635, which should return TRUE.

    Application to the test set

    On the references of ref_test.txt, the extracted DOIs can be checked without going through OpenAlex:

    doi_check <- data.frame(
  ref_n = refs $ ref_n,
  Categorie = design $ Categorie,
  doi = refs $ doi,
  doi_exists = check_doi_exists(refs $ doi),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

doi_check |>
  kable_site(
    caption = "Existence of the test set DOIs",
    col.names = c("ref_n", "Category", "Extracted DOI", "DOI exists?")
  )
    Existence of the test set DOIs
    ref_n Category Extracted DOI DOI exists?
    1

    		10.1207/s15327965pli1104_01 TRUE
    2

    We expect:

    • TRUE for the real DOIs of categories 1 and 2 (including the misattributed ones of category 2, which do exist);
    • FALSE for the fabricated DOIs of categories 3 and 4;
    • NA for references without a DOI (books, conference papers, chapters).

    Limitations of this check.

    • It verifies the existence of the DOI, not its consistency with the cited reference: that is the role of validate_references().
    • Requests are sent one at a time, with a maximum timeout of 10 seconds each and no retry on failure. On a long list, processing can therefore be slow, and a temporary service outage can produce false FALSE values.

    In a pipeline, check_doi_exists() can serve as a pre-filter to quickly identify nonexistent DOIs, before launching the more costly full validation.

    Complete pipeline

    To recap, here is the full sequence of a workflow, from preparation to selection of the best candidate:

    # 1. Prepare the references
refs <- parse_apa_text(
  system.file("extdata", "ref_test.txt", package = "CheckrefR"),
  as_ref_df = TRUE
)
# (or grobid_process_file() / grobid_process_files() for the GROBID route)

# 2. Tune the validation (optional)
checkrefr_set_defaults(doi_email = "me@example.com")

# 3. Validate
validated <- validate_references(refs)

# 4. Keep the best candidate for each reference
best <- deduplicate_references(validated)
